endorsements.quote: Algorithms should be validated across populations to ensure fairness in performance.
Monitoring should assess the fairness and equity of the algorithm output as well as the impact of the algorithm on patients, populations, and society, including data privacy and resource allocation.
Evaluate training data sets for representativeness of specific populations.
Algorithm developers should disclose types, sizes, and overall distributions in data sets used in their formulation, testing, and validation.
If biases have been identified in an algorithm, the developers, implementers, and users should disclose such biases.
Regulation should require algorithm information labels or model cards sufficient to assess design, validity, and the presence of bias.

Patients and communities, including populations who have been historically marginalized, should be engaged authentically and ethically when identifying and assessing a problem that requires use of an algorithm as part of its solution and during algorithm data selection, development, deployment, and monitoring.
It is crucial for organizations to engage stakeholders throughout the entire algorithm life cycle to ensure fairness and promote trust.
Engage patients and communities in decisions about those problems best addressed by algorithm solutions.

When unfairness is identified, bias should be mitigated using both social (eg, diverse teams and stakeholder co-development) and technical (eg, algorithmic fairness toolkits, fairness metrics, data set collection, and deimplementation) mitigation methods.

Health care delivery organizations and algorithm vendors should invest in infrastructure, governance, and teams with diverse skills and experiences to support equity and fairness in algorithm development and use.
Unfair algorithms should be deactivated, removed, or discontinued.
A structured reporting process could identify signals of emerging problems both locally and nationally and facilitate addressing the problems systematically.
There should be redress for persons and communities who have been harmed by biased algorithms.
Organizations should have an inventory of their algorithms and have local, periodic evaluations and processes that screen for and mitigate bias.
Algorithms with a higher risk of substantial harm and injustice should have stricter internal oversight by organizations and more stringent external regulation.
Institutions such as vendors and health care provider organizations should establish processes at each phase of the algorithm life cycle to promote equity and fairness.

Algorithm developers should create profiles of the data used to train the algorithm, describing distribution of key aspects of the population in the data set (eg, race and ethnicity, gender, socioeconomic status, and age); they should also make data exploration analysis readily available for independent review.

unlisted_practices: Do not deploy algorithms before validation on the impacted population.
Support underresourced institutions with limited technical capability in validating algorithms.
Inform patients when an algorithm is used in their care, including how it performs for their demographic group, and offer opt-out or alternatives where appropriate.
Regulators and accreditation bodies should mandate transparency and regular monitoring and validation of health care algorithms for equity and fairness.
Create incentives for fairness in health care algorithms.
Update reporting guidelines for algorithm research to include specific equity approaches.
Require human input in health decisions rather than allowing algorithms to make patient care decisions automatically.
Ensure algorithms respect data sovereignty, particularly for Indigenous nations.

screen.reason: Expert panel consensus framework and guiding principles from AHRQ and NIMHD for mitigating bias across the algorithm life cycle to promote health equity.
